title: Movement Disorders
summary: Parkinsonism, tremor, chorea, dystonia and more.

lessons.title: Parkinson's Disease

levels.kid:
Deep in your brain there is a tiny patch of cells that makes a helper chemical called dopamine. Dopamine is like oil in a bike chain: it helps your movements start smoothly and keep going.

In Parkinson's disease, those dopamine cells slowly wear out. With less "oil," movements get slow and stiff. A hand might shake a little while it rests in a lap, and the shaking stops when the person reaches for a cup. Walking can turn into small shuffling steps, and the face may look less expressive.

Doctors can't fix the worn-out cells yet, but medicines that add back dopamine help a lot. Exercise, like dancing or boxing practice, helps too!
levels.hs:
Parkinson's disease (PD) is a slowly progressive neurodegenerative disease. Its core problem is the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the **substantia nigra pars compacta**, a nucleus in the midbrain that sends dopamine to the striatum (part of the basal ganglia). By the time symptoms appear, a large share of these neurons is already gone.

The diagnosis is clinical. The key feature is **bradykinesia**: slowness of movement with a decrement, meaning repeated finger taps get smaller and slower. It must come with **rest tremor** and/or **rigidity**. Classic signs:
- A "pill-rolling" tremor at rest, often starting on one side
- Lead-pipe rigidity, sometimes with a "cogwheel" catch when tremor is mixed in
- Small handwriting (micrographia), soft voice, reduced facial expression
- A stooped, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing; balance problems come later

Many patients also have non-motor symptoms years before the movement problems: loss of smell, constipation, and acting out dreams during sleep (REM sleep behavior disorder). Depression and anxiety are common.

Treatment replaces or mimics dopamine. **Levodopa** (combined with carbidopa) is the most effective drug. Exercise genuinely helps mobility.
levels.college:
PD is defined clinically using the MDS criteria (2015): parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity) with supportive features, no absolute exclusions, and limited red flags. Supportive features include a clear, dramatic response to dopaminergic therapy, levodopa-induced dyskinesias, a rest tremor of a limb, and either olfactory loss or cardiac sympathetic denervation on MIBG scintigraphy.

Pathology: loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, with **Lewy bodies** and Lewy neurites containing misfolded alpha-synuclein. The striatum is deprived of dopamine. In the classic basal ganglia model, reduced D1 signaling weakens the direct (go) pathway and reduced D2 signaling disinhibits the indirect (no-go) pathway; both changes increase inhibitory output from the GPi/SNr onto the thalamus, so cortical motor programs are under-driven.

Features that point to typical PD: asymmetric onset, rest tremor, a sustained levodopa response, and slow progression over years. Imaging: routine MRI is usually normal and is used to exclude other causes. DaT-SPECT shows reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter binding in the striatum (putamen first), which separates degenerative parkinsonism from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism, but it cannot distinguish PD from atypical parkinsonism.

Genetics: most cases are sporadic; age is the biggest risk factor. Monogenic forms include SNCA (alpha-synuclein), LRRK2 (the commonest dominant form), and recessive PRKN, PINK1 and DJ-1, which tend to start young. GBA1 variants are the most common genetic risk factor.

Non-motor features: hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, orthostatic hypotension, depression, apathy, and later cognitive impairment (PD dementia).
levels.phd:
The Braak staging hypothesis proposed that Lewy pathology begins in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and the olfactory bulb, ascends through the brainstem (locus coeruleus, raphe), reaches the substantia nigra at the stage of motor symptoms, and finally spreads to the cortex. This fits the prodrome of hyposmia, constipation and REM sleep behavior disorder. Animal work shows that misfolded alpha-synuclein fibrils can template the misfolding of normal protein and travel between connected neurons in a prion-like fashion, and some rodent models show gut-to-brain spread via the vagus. The model is debated: not every brain follows Braak's sequence, and the "body-first versus brain-first" framework proposes two subtypes, with REM sleep behavior disorder and early autonomic denervation marking the body-first type.

A major advance is the **alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay** (RT-QuIC), which detects misfolded synuclein in CSF with high sensitivity and specificity, and skin biopsy for phosphorylated synuclein. These enable proposals for a biological definition (for example the SynNeurGe and neuronal synuclein disease frameworks), shifting PD from a clinical syndrome toward a defined proteinopathy.

Why are nigral neurons so vulnerable? They have huge unmyelinated axonal arbors with hundreds of thousands of synapses, autonomous pacemaking that uses L-type calcium channels and creates mitochondrial oxidative stress, and cytosolic dopamine that can oxidize. The genes PINK1 and Parkin form a mitochondrial quality-control pathway (mitophagy); LRRK2 kinase hyperactivity affects lysosomal and vesicle trafficking; GBA1 loss reduces lysosomal glucocerebrosidase, impairing synuclein clearance. Lysosomal and mitochondrial failure are therefore central themes.

Disease-modifying trials (anti-synuclein antibodies, LRRK2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists) have so far given mixed or modest results, partly because patients are enrolled after most neurons are already lost.
levels.expert:
In clinic, the diagnosis rests on examining bradykinesia correctly. Ask for finger taps, hand opening, and toe or heel taps for 10 to 15 repetitions and watch for decrement: progressive loss of amplitude and speed, or hesitations. Slowness without decrement is less specific. Check rigidity with activation (moving the opposite hand makes subtle rigidity appear). Look at the face, blink rate, voice, writing, arm swing and turning. Do a pull test for postural instability, standing behind the patient ready to catch.

Red flags that should make you doubt PD: early falls within three years, poor or no levodopa response, symmetric onset with no tremor, rapid progression, early severe autonomic failure, vertical gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, early dementia or hallucinations, and stridor or severe early swallowing problems. Always review the medication list: antipsychotics and some anti-nausea drugs (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) block D2 receptors and cause drug-induced parkinsonism, which is usually symmetric and improves after stopping the drug, though recovery may take months.

In a young patient (under about 40) with parkinsonism or a movement disorder, consider Wilson disease and genetic forms.

Management is tailored to symptoms and life goals. Levodopa is not "saved for later"; delaying it does not prevent complications, and the benefit to quality of life is large. Over years, fluctuations develop: wearing-off before the next dose, unpredictable "on-off" swings, and peak-dose dyskinesias. Strategies include adjusting timing, adding MAO-B or COMT inhibitors, dopamine agonists, and later device-aided therapies such as deep brain stimulation or continuous infusions.

Watch for dopamine agonist side effects, especially impulse control disorders (compulsive gambling, shopping, eating), and ask about them at every visit. Physical therapy, speech therapy and high-intensity exercise are evidence-based. Hospitalized PD patients need their medications on time; missed doses can cause severe rigidity.

keyPoints: PD: loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein).
Diagnosis is clinical: bradykinesia with decrement plus rest tremor and/or rigidity.
Non-motor prodrome: loss of smell, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, mood changes.
DaT-SPECT shows presynaptic dopamine loss but does not separate PD from atypical parkinsonism.
Levodopa is the most effective drug; fluctuations and dyskinesias appear over years.
Red flags: early falls, poor levodopa response, gaze palsy, early autonomic failure.

lessons.title: Atypical Parkinsonism

levels.kid:
Some people have slow, stiff movements like Parkinson's disease, but something a bit different is going on in their brain. Doctors call these "Parkinson's look-alikes."

One look-alike makes people fall backward a lot and makes it hard to move their eyes up and down. Another one makes it hard for the body to control blood pressure, so people feel dizzy when they stand up. A third one can make one hand act like it has a mind of its own.

The big clue is that the usual Parkinson's medicine doesn't help much. Doctors look closely at eyes, balance and the brain scan to tell which look-alike it is, so they can plan the best care.
levels.hs:
"Atypical parkinsonism" (also called Parkinson-plus syndromes) means a parkinsonian syndrome that is not Parkinson's disease. These conditions usually progress faster, respond poorly to levodopa, and have extra signs. The main ones:

- **Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP):** early falls (often backward), stiff upright posture, and trouble moving the eyes vertically, especially looking down. The face can look surprised or staring. It is a tauopathy (abnormal tau protein).
- **Multiple system atrophy (MSA):** parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia combined with **autonomic failure**: fainting from low blood pressure on standing, bladder problems, and reduced sweating. Loud snoring or noisy breathing (stridor) can occur. It is a synucleinopathy with protein clumps in glial cells.
- **Corticobasal syndrome (CBS):** very asymmetric stiffness, jerks and loss of skilled movements (apraxia) of one limb. The "alien limb" phenomenon, where a hand moves on its own, is a famous sign.
- **Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB):** early dementia with fluctuating alertness, vivid visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.

Telling them apart matters for prognosis, safety and planning. People with DLB, for example, can react badly to some antipsychotic drugs.
levels.college:
The atypical parkinsonisms are divided by the misfolded protein: **synucleinopathies** (MSA, dementia with Lewy bodies, and PD itself) and **tauopathies** (PSP and corticobasal degeneration).

PSP (Richardson syndrome) features early postural instability with falls in the first year, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (downgaze is most diagnostic; slowed vertical saccades precede the palsy), axial more than limb rigidity, a frontal dysexecutive syndrome, and pseudobulbar signs. Because the palsy is supranuclear, the vestibulo-ocular reflex (doll's eyes) can still move the eyes. MRI may show midbrain atrophy with a preserved pons: the "hummingbird" or "penguin" sign on midsagittal images and the "morning glory" sign axially.

MSA is subdivided into MSA-P (parkinsonian) and MSA-C (cerebellar). Autonomic failure is central: neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, urinary urge incontinence or retention, and reduced sweating. Other clues are inspiratory stridor, antecollis, cold blue hands, and REM sleep behavior disorder. MRI may show the "hot cross bun" sign in the pons (MSA-C), middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy, and putaminal changes. Pathology: glial cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes.

Corticobasal syndrome is a clinical picture (asymmetric rigidity, limb dystonia, myoclonus, ideomotor apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb) that can come from several pathologies: corticobasal degeneration, PSP, Alzheimer disease, or others. So the syndrome name and the pathology name are kept separate.

Dementia with Lewy bodies: dementia beginning before or within a year of parkinsonism, with fluctuations, visual hallucinations and REM sleep behavior disorder. Neuroleptic sensitivity can be severe.

Clues against PD overall: symmetric onset, absent rest tremor, early falls, rapid progression, poor or transient levodopa response.
levels.phd:
Pathologically, the tauopathies differ by isoform and cell type. PSP and corticobasal degeneration are 4-repeat (4R) tauopathies. PSP is defined by tufted astrocytes plus neurofibrillary tangles in the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, substantia nigra and brainstem; corticobasal degeneration by astrocytic plaques and ballooned neurons in frontoparietal cortex. Cryo-electron microscopy has shown that tau filaments adopt disease-specific folds, so the same protein forms distinct conformational strains in PSP, corticobasal degeneration, Alzheimer disease and Pick disease. A similar story exists for synuclein: MSA filaments differ from those in Lewy body disease, and MSA seeds behave differently in amplification assays, which is being explored as a way to separate MSA from PD in life.

Why do glial cells carry the inclusions in MSA? The leading idea is that oligodendrocytes take up or mis-handle synuclein, lose myelin-supporting function, and trigger secondary neurodegeneration along olivopontocerebellar and striatonigral pathways. That anatomy explains the combination of ataxia and parkinsonism.

Diagnostic criteria have been updated: the MDS PSP criteria (2017) recognize several phenotypes beyond Richardson syndrome, such as PSP-parkinsonism (which can mimic PD early and respond partly to levodopa), PSP with progressive gait freezing, and PSP-corticobasal syndrome. The MDS MSA criteria (2022) introduced categories including "clinically established" and "clinically probable" MSA, plus a research category for early cases, and emphasize MRI markers.

Imaging research adds tools: FDG-PET hypometabolism patterns (midbrain and medial frontal in PSP, putamen and cerebellum in MSA, asymmetric frontoparietal in CBS), tau PET (limited for 4R tau), and the MR parkinsonism index, which compares pons and midbrain areas and cerebellar peduncle widths.

Therapeutically, anti-tau antibody trials in PSP were negative, illustrating how hard it is to treat these diseases once clinically evident.
levels.expert:
In practice, the question in a new parkinsonian patient is "PD or not?" Most errors come from not looking for the extra signs. Examine vertical saccades, not only pursuit: slow vertical saccades or square-wave jerks are early PSP clues. Watch the patient rise from a chair (a "rocket sign," standing up suddenly and impulsively, is PSP-like). Ask about falls specifically, and time them: falls in year one are a red flag.

Always measure lying and standing blood pressure. A sustained drop on standing with little rise in heart rate suggests neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, pointing to MSA (or PD with autonomic failure, or DLB). Ask about bladder symptoms early, stridor at night (a sleep partner may notice), and dysphagia. In MSA, nocturnal stridor is a risk for sudden death in sleep and may need assessment by ENT or sleep services.

A levodopa trial is still worthwhile: some patients with atypical syndromes gain partial benefit, and a dramatic sustained response is strong evidence for PD. MSA patients may develop odd facial and neck dyskinesias on levodopa.

In suspected Lewy body dementia, avoid typical antipsychotics because of severe sensitivity reactions; cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations. Treat orthostatic hypotension with nonpharmacological steps (fluids, salt, compression, head-up tilt of the bed) and, when needed, drugs such as midodrine or droxidopa, while watching for supine hypertension.

Deep brain stimulation is generally not helpful in atypical parkinsonism, which is one reason the distinction matters before surgery. Prognosis conversations, swallowing and speech therapy, fall prevention, and early palliative care involvement are core parts of care. Because diagnosis is clinical and phenotypes overlap, revisit it at every visit; the true diagnosis often becomes clear only over time.

keyPoints: Atypical parkinsonism: faster course, poor levodopa response, extra signs.
PSP: early backward falls, vertical (especially downward) gaze palsy, midbrain atrophy (hummingbird sign); 4R tauopathy.
MSA: parkinsonism or ataxia plus autonomic failure; glial synuclein inclusions; hot cross bun sign.
Corticobasal syndrome: asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, alien limb; several possible pathologies.
Dementia with Lewy bodies: early dementia, fluctuations, visual hallucinations, antipsychotic sensitivity.

lessons.title: Tremor

levels.kid:
A tremor is a shake that a body part can't stop, like a phone buzzing on a table. Everyone has a tiny shake that's too small to notice. It gets bigger when we're cold, scared or very tired.

Doctors sort tremors by when they happen. A resting tremor shakes when the hand is relaxed in a lap. An action tremor shakes when you use the hand, like holding a glass of water or writing your name.

The most common shaky-hands condition is called essential tremor. It often runs in families and makes it hard to drink from a full cup or write neatly. Doctors watch the shake carefully and ask simple questions to find the cause.
levels.hs:
A **tremor** is an involuntary, rhythmic, oscillating movement of a body part. Doctors classify tremors by when they appear:
- **Rest tremor:** present when the limb is fully supported and relaxed; typical of Parkinson's disease.
- **Postural tremor:** appears when holding a position against gravity, like arms stretched forward.
- **Kinetic (intention) tremor:** appears during movement, and an intention tremor gets worse as the hand approaches a target, like touching your nose. This points to the **cerebellum**.

**Essential tremor (ET)** is the most common movement disorder. It is a bilateral action tremor (postural and kinetic) of the hands and forearms, sometimes with head ("yes-yes" or "no-no") or voice tremor. It is often inherited (autosomal dominant pattern in many families), and many patients notice that a small amount of alcohol temporarily reduces it, an old clinical observation rather than a treatment.

**Enhanced physiological tremor** is an exaggeration of the normal fine tremor, caused by anxiety, caffeine, fatigue, an overactive thyroid, low blood sugar, or medications such as asthma inhalers or some antidepressants.

Doctors examine the tremor at rest, in posture, during finger-to-nose, while writing and drawing a spiral, and they check thyroid function. Treatment depends on how much the tremor disturbs daily life.
levels.college:
Tremor classification (MDS consensus 2018) uses two axes. Axis 1 is the clinical syndrome: age at onset, history, body distribution, activation condition, and associated signs. Axis 2 is the cause: genetic, acquired or idiopathic.

Activation conditions: rest tremor (often 3 to 6 Hz, Parkinson's disease), postural tremor, kinetic tremor (simple or intention), task-specific tremor (for example primary writing tremor), and isometric tremor. Orthostatic tremor is a high-frequency (about 13 to 18 Hz) tremor of the legs on standing that causes unsteadiness relieved by sitting or walking; it may be felt more than seen and is confirmed by surface EMG.

Essential tremor is defined as an isolated, bilateral upper-limb action tremor present for at least three years, with or without tremor in other places (head, voice, lower limbs), and without other neurological signs such as dystonia, ataxia or parkinsonism. "Essential tremor plus" describes ET with soft additional signs such as mild impaired tandem gait or questionable dystonic posturing. ET usually has a frequency of 4 to 12 Hz, with higher frequencies in younger people.

Distinguishing features:
- PD: asymmetric rest tremor, re-emergent tremor after a latency when holding a posture, with bradykinesia and rigidity.
- ET: symmetric action tremor, often with family history; spiral drawing shows a consistent axis.
- Dystonic tremor: irregular, jerky, position-sensitive, with a null point; may improve with a sensory trick.
- Cerebellar tremor: low-frequency intention tremor with dysmetria, ataxia and nystagmus.
- Holmes tremor: a rest, postural and intention tremor caused by a midbrain or thalamic lesion, often weeks to months after a stroke.
- Functional tremor: variable frequency, distractibility, entrainment to a rhythm tapped by the other hand.

Work-up: medication review, thyroid function, glucose, and in young patients copper studies for Wilson disease.
levels.phd:
Tremor emerges from oscillating networks. The cerebello-thalamo-cortical loop is central: cerebellar output through the dentate nucleus reaches the ventral intermediate nucleus (Vim) of the thalamus and then motor cortex. In essential tremor, rhythmic activity in this loop is thought to be driven by abnormal olivocerebellar and cerebellar circuitry. The harmaline animal model produces tremor by making inferior olive neurons fire synchronously, supporting the olive as a pacemaker, although human pathology emphasizes cerebellar changes.

Neuropathology studies of ET brains (debated) report Purkinje cell loss, swollen Purkinje axons ("torpedoes"), and climbing fiber changes, leading to the view that ET may be a cerebellar degenerative disorder in at least some patients. Critics note overlap with normal aging and inconsistent findings. GABA dysfunction is another theme, because GABA-enhancing agents such as primidone and some sedatives can reduce ET.

PD rest tremor follows a "dimmer-switch" model: the basal ganglia trigger tremor episodes (the switch), while the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit sets the tremor amplitude (the dimmer). This helps explain why rest tremor responds less predictably to levodopa than bradykinesia does, and why Vim stimulation can abolish PD tremor without improving bradykinesia.

Physiological tremor has a mechanical component (determined by limb mass and stiffness, so adding weight lowers its frequency) and a central neural component (around 8 to 12 Hz, unchanged by loading). Loading tests with accelerometry can separate these.

Genetics of ET is frustrating despite strong heritability: linkage loci and candidate genes (for example in TENM4 and FUS families) explain few cases, suggesting heterogeneity and a group of disorders rather than one disease.

Quantitative tools such as accelerometry, EMG, and spiral analysis help separate tremor types and measure treatment effects in trials.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, look for the tremor in all activation states: hands resting in the lap while the patient counts backward (distraction brings out PD rest tremor), arms outstretched, the "wing-beating" posture with fingers pointing at each other, finger-to-nose, spiral drawing, writing a sentence, and pouring water between cups. Ask about onset, family history, response to alcohol (as a clue only), caffeine, medications and thyroid symptoms.

Common pitfalls:
- Calling every older person's tremor "PD." A symmetric postural and kinetic tremor with family history and no bradykinesia is ET.
- Missing dystonic tremor of the head, which is often irregular and associated with abnormal neck posture (cervical dystonia).
- Missing drug-induced tremor from valproate, lithium, amiodarone, beta-agonists, some antidepressants, or tacrolimus.
- Missing Wilson disease in a young patient, particularly with a proximal "wing-beating" tremor, liver disease or psychiatric symptoms.

Treatment of ET is symptomatic and driven by disability, not by the tremor's appearance. First-line drugs are propranolol (avoid in asthma) and primidone; topiramate and gabapentin are alternatives. Weighted utensils and occupational therapy help.

For disabling, medication-refractory ET, options are:
- Deep brain stimulation of the Vim thalamus (or the posterior subthalamic area), which is adjustable and can be done on both sides.
- MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy, an incisionless lesion of Vim. It is usually done on one side first; staged bilateral treatment is now possible in selected patients but carries more risk of speech and balance problems.

Surgical selection includes confirming the diagnosis, checking cognition and mood, and setting realistic expectations: head and voice tremor respond less well than hand tremor.

keyPoints: Tremor: involuntary rhythmic oscillation; classify by rest, postural or kinetic activation.
Essential tremor: bilateral action tremor of the arms for at least three years, often familial.
Intention tremor worsening near a target points to the cerebellum.
Enhanced physiological tremor: anxiety, caffeine, hyperthyroidism, low glucose, drugs.
Refractory ET: DBS of the Vim thalamus or focused ultrasound thalamotomy.

lessons.title: Chorea, Dystonia & Tics

levels.kid:
Some movement problems make the body move too much instead of too little.

Chorea is when the body makes little dance-like wiggles that flow from one part to another, like a puppet whose strings get tugged by surprise. Dystonia is when muscles squeeze too long and twist a body part into a stuck position, like a neck that keeps turning to one side. Tics are quick moves or sounds, like blinking or sniffing, that a person feels a strong urge to do. They can hold them in for a bit, like holding in a sneeze.

Lots of kids have tics that come and go. Doctors help figure out each kind and find ways to make daily life easier.
levels.hs:
**Hyperkinetic** movement disorders produce too much involuntary movement. Three important types:

**Chorea** (Greek for "dance") is brief, irregular, flowing movements that jump unpredictably from one body part to another. Patients may look fidgety and may blend jerks into purposeful-looking gestures. The best-known cause is **Huntington disease (HD)**, an inherited condition caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene, with chorea, behavior and mood changes, and dementia. Other causes include Sydenham chorea after strep infection (linked to rheumatic fever), pregnancy, lupus, high blood sugar and some drugs.

**Dystonia** means sustained or intermittent muscle contractions that cause twisting movements or abnormal postures. It can be focal (one region, like cervical dystonia twisting the neck, blepharospasm forcing the eyes shut, or writer's cramp), segmental or generalized. Many patients discover a **sensory trick** (geste antagoniste): lightly touching the chin can relieve neck dystonia.

**Tics** are sudden, repetitive, non-rhythmic movements (blinking, shrugging) or sounds (throat clearing, sniffing). They are usually preceded by an urge and can be briefly suppressed. **Tourette syndrome** is defined by multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic for more than a year, starting before age 18. Tics usually peak in early adolescence and often improve by adulthood.
levels.college:
Phenomenology comes first: name the movement before naming the disease.

Chorea results from reduced indirect-pathway output. In early Huntington disease, striatal medium spiny neurons of the indirect pathway (D2, enkephalin) degenerate first, disinhibiting the thalamus and producing excess movement. HD is autosomal dominant with full penetrance at 40 or more CAG repeats (36 to 39 is reduced penetrance). Anticipation occurs, especially with paternal transmission, because the repeat expands in sperm. MRI shows caudate atrophy with boxcar-shaped lateral ventricles. Other causes: Sydenham chorea (anti-basal ganglia autoimmunity after group A strep), chorea gravidarum, antiphospholipid syndrome and lupus, nonketotic hyperglycemia (hemichorea with putaminal T1 hyperintensity), polycythemia, neuroacanthocytosis, and drugs (levodopa, stimulants, some anticonvulsants). Hemiballismus, violent flinging of one side, classically follows a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

Dystonia is classified on two axes: clinical features (age at onset, body distribution, temporal pattern, isolated or combined with other movement disorders) and cause. Early-onset generalized isolated dystonia often relates to the TOR1A (DYT1) GAG deletion, typically starting in a limb in childhood and spreading. Dopa-responsive dystonia (GCH1) presents in childhood with leg dystonia that worsens through the day and responds dramatically to low-dose levodopa; every child with unexplained dystonia deserves a levodopa trial. Acute dystonic reactions (oculogyric crisis, torticollis) can follow D2-blocking drugs.

Tics: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor and at least one vocal tic for more than one year, onset before 18. Coexisting ADHD and OCD are common and often more disabling than the tics. Tics differ from compulsions and stereotypies (rhythmic, no premonitory urge, typical of autism).

Myoclonus (shock-like jerks) and functional movement disorders complete the hyperkinetic differential.
levels.phd:
Huntington disease illustrates how a protein gains toxic function. The CAG repeat encodes a polyglutamine tract in huntingtin; expanded polyglutamine promotes misfolding and aggregation, impairs transcription (for example of BDNF), and disrupts axonal transport and mitochondrial function. Genome-wide association studies of age at onset identified DNA mismatch repair genes (such as MSH3 and FAN1), shifting attention to **somatic repeat expansion**: the CAG tract keeps lengthening in vulnerable striatal neurons during life, and toxicity may begin only once a threshold is crossed. This reframes therapy toward slowing somatic expansion as well as lowering huntingtin. Huntingtin-lowering antisense oligonucleotides had a disappointing phase 3 result, and AAV-delivered gene therapies are under study, with early reports of slowed progression in small trials that still need confirmation.

Dystonia is now seen as a network disorder rather than purely a basal ganglia disease. Evidence includes reduced surround inhibition in motor cortex, abnormal sensorimotor integration (explaining sensory tricks), maladaptive plasticity (focal task-specific dystonia in musicians and writers after intense repetitive practice), and cerebellar involvement. Many dystonia genes converge on shared pathways: TOR1A affects the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum, THAP1 is a transcription factor that regulates TOR1A, and GNAL and ANO3 affect striatal signaling. Pallidal DBS works for some genetic dystonias (TOR1A responds very well) but less for others.

In tics, the premonitory urge is a key concept: tics may be partly a learned response that relieves an uncomfortable sensation, which is why behavioral therapy (CBIT: awareness training and a competing response) works. Imaging suggests altered cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits and the insula's role in urge sensation. Tics' natural history, with improvement in late adolescence, may reflect maturation of frontal control networks.
levels.expert:
In clinic, describe what you see in words before choosing a label; video recordings help, especially for paroxysmal events.

Chorea work-up: family history (it may be hidden by early death, misattributed paternity or adoption), medication list, glucose, thyroid, full blood count and smear (acanthocytes), autoimmune screen including antiphospholipid antibodies, and in children recent strep infection and an echocardiogram for carditis. Predictive genetic testing for HD in someone without symptoms follows a structured protocol with genetic counseling, psychological support and time to decide; it is generally not offered to minors because the result cannot change care and removes their future choice. Treatment of chorea is symptomatic (VMAT2 inhibitors such as tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine or valbenazine, or antipsychotics), but chorea often matters less to patients than depression, irritability, apathy and cognition. Screen for depression carefully; suicide risk in HD is elevated.

Dystonia: always try levodopa in childhood-onset dystonia to avoid missing dopa-responsive dystonia, and exclude Wilson disease in young patients. Botulinum toxin injected into overactive muscles is first-line for focal dystonias such as cervical dystonia and blepharospasm; EMG or ultrasound guidance improves accuracy. Anticholinergic drugs are used mainly in younger patients. Pallidal (GPi) DBS helps generalized and cervical dystonia, with improvement building over months, unlike the immediate effect in tremor. Status dystonicus is an emergency that can cause muscle breakdown and needs intensive care.

Tics: education is the most powerful first step; many families only need reassurance that tics wax and wane and often improve. Treat when tics cause pain, social harm or disruption. First-line is behavioral therapy (CBIT); medicines include alpha-2 agonists and, for severe tics, other options. Address coexisting ADHD, OCD and anxiety, which often drive impairment more than the tics do.

keyPoints: Chorea: brief, irregular, flowing movements; Huntington disease is the classic cause.
Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT; caudate atrophy; anticipation.
Dystonia: sustained contractions causing twisting postures; sensory tricks; botulinum toxin for focal forms.
Child with dystonia: always try levodopa (dopa-responsive dystonia).
Tics: urge-driven, suppressible; Tourette = multiple motor + vocal tics over a year, onset before 18.

lessons.title: Treatment & DBS

levels.kid:
Doctors have a toolbox for movement problems. First come medicines, like ones that add back dopamine for Parkinson's. Then there's exercise and therapy that help people walk, talk and write better.

When medicines stop working well, surgeons can use deep brain stimulation, called DBS. They place a super-thin wire deep in the brain. The wire connects to a little battery under the skin of the chest, like a pacemaker for the brain. It sends tiny, steady signals that calm the messy brain messages causing shakes or stiffness.

The coolest part: doctors can adjust it with a tablet, and the patient is often awake during surgery so the team can check it's working!
levels.hs:
Treating movement disorders combines medicines, therapy and sometimes surgery.

**Medicines for Parkinson's disease:**
- **Levodopa** (with carbidopa): converted to dopamine in the brain; the strongest drug.
- **Dopamine agonists** (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch): stimulate dopamine receptors directly.
- **MAO-B inhibitors** (rasagiline, safinamide) and **COMT inhibitors** (entacapone, opicapone): slow dopamine or levodopa breakdown.
- **Amantadine**: reduces dyskinesias.

Over years, the levodopa benefit shortens ("wearing off") and extra wriggling movements (**dyskinesias**) can appear.

**Deep brain stimulation (DBS)** is neurosurgery in which electrodes are placed in a deep brain target and connected to a pulse generator under the collarbone. Common targets:
- **Subthalamic nucleus (STN)** or **globus pallidus internus (GPi)** for Parkinson's disease
- **Ventral intermediate nucleus (Vim)** of the thalamus for essential tremor
- **GPi** for dystonia

DBS does not cure the disease or stop it progressing, but it can greatly reduce tremor, fluctuations and dyskinesias. The best candidates with PD have a clear levodopa response, because DBS generally improves the symptoms levodopa improves (tremor is the exception, responding even when levodopa doesn't help it). Risks include bleeding, infection and speech or mood changes.
levels.college:
Medical therapy in PD: levodopa has a short plasma half-life, so as presynaptic buffering is lost, the clinical response follows plasma levels, producing motor fluctuations (wearing-off, delayed-on, sudden off) and peak-dose dyskinesias. Strategies: fractionate doses, add COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, add an agonist, use amantadine for dyskinesia, or move to continuous delivery (levodopa intestinal gel through a gastrostomy, subcutaneous foslevodopa/foscarbidopa infusion, or apomorphine infusion). Levodopa absorption competes with dietary large neutral amino acids, so protein-rich meals can blunt doses.

DBS selection for PD (the CAPSIT/CAPIT tradition): idiopathic PD, typically at least four to five years of disease, a robust levodopa challenge response (often an improvement of at least 30% in the MDS-UPDRS part III), troublesome fluctuations, dyskinesias or medication-refractory tremor, no significant dementia, and controlled psychiatric illness. The axial symptoms that do not respond to levodopa (freezing in the "on" state, balance, speech) usually do not respond to DBS either.

Targets: STN DBS often allows a larger medication reduction; GPi DBS has a direct anti-dyskinetic effect and may be preferred when cognition, mood or medication flexibility are concerns. Vim DBS treats tremor of almost any cause but not bradykinesia.

Procedure: targets are planned on MRI (direct visualization or atlas-based coordinates) using a stereotactic frame or frameless system. Microelectrode recording identifies characteristic firing (STN neurons fire fast and irregularly with beta oscillations; leaving the STN inferiorly reaches the substantia nigra reticulata), and intraoperative test stimulation checks for benefit and side effects in an awake patient. Asleep surgery with intraoperative MRI or CT verification is an accepted alternative.

Programming chooses contacts, amplitude, pulse width and frequency (usually high frequency, about 130 Hz), and directional leads can steer current away from structures that cause side effects.
levels.phd:
How DBS works is still debated. High-frequency stimulation mimics a lesion clinically, yet it does not simply silence neurons: it activates axons near the electrode (both efferent fibers and passing fibers), drives somata into regular firing patterns, and overrides pathological rhythms with a regular, information-poor signal ("informational lesion"). In PD, exaggerated beta-band (13 to 30 Hz) synchrony in the STN and cortex correlates with bradykinesia and rigidity, and both levodopa and DBS suppress it. Optogenetic work in rodents suggested that stimulating cortical afferents to the STN (the hyperdirect pathway) can be sufficient for benefit.

These findings drive **adaptive (closed-loop) DBS**: sensing-enabled devices record local field potentials and adjust stimulation according to beta power. Commercial systems now allow adaptive stimulation, and trials suggest comparable or better symptom control with less energy and fewer side effects, though which biomarker suits which patient remains an active question. Other developments: directional segmented leads, interleaving programs, and connectomics, in which normative tractography maps the fibers activated by each contact to predict outcome (for example, hyperdirect connectivity to motor cortex predicting STN DBS benefit).

Lesioning has re-emerged through **MRI-guided focused ultrasound**, which treats tremor by thalamotomy and has been studied for unilateral pallidotomy and subthalamotomy in PD. Lesions are permanent and not adjustable, which shapes patient selection.

Restorative strategies remain experimental. Fetal mesencephalic grafts in the 1990s and 2000s gave variable results and graft-induced dyskinesias, and Lewy pathology was later found inside grafted neurons, suggesting host-to-graft spread. Stem cell-derived dopaminergic neuron transplants entered early-phase trials with encouraging safety and imaging signals. Gene therapies deliver enzymes (AADC) or growth factors (GDNF-family) with mixed results.

DBS beyond movement disorders includes approved or investigational uses for epilepsy (anterior thalamus), OCD and depression.
levels.expert:
A DBS program is a team: movement disorders neurologist, functional neurosurgeon, neuropsychologist, psychiatrist, nurse programmers and therapists. The most important decision is selection, and most poor outcomes trace back to it: wrong diagnosis (atypical parkinsonism), cognitive impairment, untreated depression, or expectations the surgery cannot meet ("Will it fix my balance?" usually no).

Pre-operative work-up: a formal levodopa challenge (off medication overnight, then a suprathreshold dose with MDS-UPDRS scoring), neuropsychological testing, psychiatric assessment, MRI to look for vascular disease or atrophy, and a frank discussion of goals. Risks to discuss include intracerebral hemorrhage (on the order of 1 to 2% in many series), infection or erosion of hardware, lead misplacement requiring revision, speech and gait worsening, weight gain, and mood change, including depression or apathy after medication reduction and, rarely, impulsivity or mania from stimulation near limbic STN regions.

Surgical pearls: plan trajectories that avoid sulci, vessels and ventricles; check brain shift from CSF loss, which can move targets by millimeters; correlate microelectrode recording, test stimulation and imaging; and confirm lead position by post-operative CT fused to the planning MRI.

Programming pearls: benefits for tremor and rigidity appear within seconds to minutes, bradykinesia over minutes to hours, dystonia over weeks to months. Stimulation-induced side effects map onto anatomy around the target: tonic muscle contraction (internal capsule), paresthesias (sensory thalamus or medial lemniscus), diplopia or eye deviation (oculomotor fibers medial to the STN), and dysarthria. Reduce medications in step with stimulation to avoid dyskinesias.

Safety: patients need a device card, MRI only under manufacturer-approved conditions, and caution with diathermy. Abrupt loss of stimulation (battery depletion, hardware failure) in PD or dystonia can cause severe rebound and is managed as an urgent problem.

keyPoints: PD drugs: levodopa (strongest), dopamine agonists, MAO-B and COMT inhibitors, amantadine for dyskinesia.
Long-term levodopa: wearing-off fluctuations and peak-dose dyskinesias.
DBS targets: STN or GPi for PD, Vim for essential tremor, GPi for dystonia.
Best PD DBS candidates: clear levodopa response, no dementia, controlled mood disorders.
DBS improves what levodopa improves (plus tremor) but not levodopa-resistant balance or speech.
